doc.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

title: Kansas City and the changing jazz audience
summary: Today's festival sets, playing Kansas City with Dinah and Bostic, and how suburbanization drained city club audiences, now partly rebuilt by colleges.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Wow. Well this has really been fascinating. I’m so glad that we were able to have you come over and join us. You are playing today again?
Today, yes. I’m doing the Kansas City Seven, and then the big band, The Juggernauts.
Did you have occasion to play in Kansas City?

Oh yeah. With Dinah, with Bostic, I mean those were dances, but with Dinah Washington we would play. We’d do some one-nighters and we did work a club that was called the Blue Orchid or the Orchid Room or something. Yeah I liked Kansas City. It was a swinging town.
I think there’s a movie coming out about it now or something.

Really? All the major cities, Kansas City, Chicago, was whew, oh boy. just — New Orleans, L.A., they was all over then. Because you see you’re looking at Washington was a big mecca. But you see at that time people lived in pockets, so everything that was within that pocket flourished, the stores and shops and everything. When the suburbs started becoming the vogue thing and would start expanding all these people who were

patrons started moving out. But once you get 15 miles out of town and you go to work, you don’t feel like coming all the way back in. And this is how, to a certain point, some of the patrons was lost because people were expanding their lives and in expanding their lives they was also expanding the distance from what they were from. And so consequently what happened is that then the clubs had to wait for the new people to come in and the new people were not actually seasoned veterans of jazz yet, they had to convert them. But the advantage, the thing that’s helping that has been the colleges and with the various, all the music that’s going on at colleges, and educating the kids there, then they’re starting to get the younger crowd.
